title: Πέπλος Ἀθήνῃ
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The two men take hands and part friends, and the poet remarks that Zeus took Glaucus’ wits, since he gave gold armour for bronze, a hundred oxen’s worth for nine. Hector reaches the Scaean Gates and the oak, and the Trojan wives and daughters run round him asking after their men; he tells them all to pray. In Priam’s house, with its fifty chambers for his sons and twelve for his daughters’ husbands, his mother meets him, takes his hand and urges him to wait while she brings wine for a libation. He refuses: he would not pour wine to Zeus with unwashed hands, spattered with blood, and wine might unnerve him. She is to gather the old women, take the finest of her robes to Athena’s temple, lay it on the goddess’s knees and promise twelve heifers if Athena will keep Diomedes from Troy, while he goes to call Paris, whom he wishes dead. Hecuba chooses a Sidonian robe; the priestess Theano opens the temple, lays the robe on Athena’s knees and prays for Diomedes to fall before the gates, but Athena refuses. Hector goes to Paris’ house, where he finds him busy with his armour while Helen sits among her maids, and rebukes him: the war is burning round the town on his account.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσαντε καθ’ ἵππων ἀΐξαντε
χεῖράς τ’ ἀλλήλων λαβέτην καὶ πιστώσαντο·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsante kath’ hippōn aïxante
cheiras t’ allēlōn labetēn kai pistōsanto·
sentences.l:
So then, the two having spoken, from the horses having leapt down,
the hands of each other they took, the two, and pledged themselves;
sentences.i: So the two spoke, and leapt down from their chariots, took each other’s hands, and pledged their faith.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσαντε ‘so then, the two having spoken’ closes the meeting of Glaucus and Diomedes, and the participles φωνήσαντε and ἀΐξαντε and the verb λαβέτην are duals, the Greek number for a pair. ἵππων ‘horses’ stands for the chariots they drove. πιστώσαντο is a plural middle, ‘made themselves sure of each other’, that is, they gave pledges.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ αὖτε Γλαύκῳ Κρονίδης φρένας ἐξέλετο Ζεύς,
ὃς πρὸς Τυδεΐδην Διομήδεα τεύχε’ ἄμειβε
χρύσεα χαλκείων, ἑκατόμβοι’ ἐννεαβοίων.
sentences.tr:
enth’ aute Glaukōi Kronidēs phrenas exeleto Zeus,
hos pros Tydeïdēn Diomēdea teuche’ ameibe
chrysea chalkeiōn, hekatomboi’ enneaboiōn.
sentences.l:
Then, in turn, from Glaucus the wits took away the son of Cronus, Zeus,
who with the son of Tydeus, Diomedes, armour was exchanging,
gold for bronze, worth a hundred oxen for worth nine oxen.
sentences.i: Then Zeus, the son of Cronus, took the wits from Glaucus, who was exchanging armour with Diomedes, the son of Tydeus: gold for bronze, armour worth a hundred oxen for armour worth nine.
sentences.n: Here the poet speaks in his own voice: ἔνθ’ αὖτε ‘then, in turn’. Γλαύκῳ is a dative of the man who loses, ‘from Glaucus’, and φρένας ἐξέλετο ‘took out the wits’ says Zeus made him a fool. ἄμειβε is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘was exchanging’. χρύσεα χαλκείων is a genitive of price, ‘gold for bronze’, and ἑκατόμβοι’ ἐννεαβοίων measures each side in oxen: the neuter plural ἑκατόμβοι(α) ‘worth a hundred’ against the genitive plural ἐννεαβοίων ‘worth nine’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ὡς Σκαιάς τε πύλας καὶ φηγὸν ἵκανεν,
ἀμφ’ ἄρα μιν Τρώων ἄλοχοι θέον ἠδὲ θύγατρες
εἰρόμεναι παῖδάς τε κασιγνήτους τε ἔτας τε
καὶ πόσιας·
sentences.tr:
Hektōr d’ hōs Skaias te pylas kai phēgon hikanen,
amph’ ara min Trōōn alochoi theon ēde thygatres
eiromenai paidas te kasignētous te etas te
kai posias·
sentences.l:
And Hector, when to the Scaean Gates and the oak he came,
about him then the Trojans’ wives ran, and daughters,
asking after children and brothers and kinsmen
and husbands;
sentences.i: When Hector came to the Scaean Gates and the oak, the wives and daughters of the Trojans ran round him, asking after their children, brothers, kinsmen and husbands;
sentences.n: Σκαιάς … πύλας ‘the Scaean Gates’ is a name, usually guessed to mean ‘left-hand’ gates (σκαιός ‘left’). φηγόν is an oak (the English ‘beech’ is a false friend), a landmark by the gate. ὡς … ἵκανεν ‘when he came to’ opens the sentence, and ἀμφ’ … θέον ‘ran about’ splits the preposition from the verb. εἰρόμεναι ‘asking about’ takes four accusatives, of which ἔτας is the plural of ἔτης ‘kinsman’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἔπειτα θεοῖς εὔχεσθαι ἀνώγει
πάσας ἑξείης·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ epeita theois euchesthai anōgei
pasas hexeiēs·
sentences.l:
and he then the gods to pray bade,
all of them, in order;
sentences.i: and he told them then to pray to the gods, all of them in turn;
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ ‘and he’ uses the article as a pronoun, and ἀνώγει is ‘he bade’, followed by the infinitive εὔχεσθαι ‘to pray’. θεοῖς is the dative of the god prayed to. πάσας ‘all’ is feminine, so it means all the women; ἑξείης ‘in order’ means one after another.

sentences.t: πολλῇσι δὲ κήδε’ ἐφῆπτο.
sentences.tr: pollēisi de kēde’ ephēpto.
sentences.l: and on many sorrows had been fastened.
sentences.i: and sorrows had been fastened upon many of them.
sentences.n: πολλῇσι ‘on many’ (the women) is a dative plural in -ῃσι. κήδε’ ἐφῆπτο is ‘sorrows had been fastened on’, a pluperfect passive of ἐφάπτω; the picture is of griefs and fears tied to people like weights. The poet does not say whose men are already dead.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ Πριάμοιο δόμον περικαλλέ’ ἵκανε
ξεστῇς αἰθούσῃσι τετυγμένον·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē Priamoio domon perikalle’ hikane
xestēis aithousēisi tetygmenon·
sentences.l:
But when to Priam’s house, very fair, he came,
made with polished colonnades;
sentences.i: But when he came to Priam’s very fair house, built with polished colonnades;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ‘but when’ begins a long sentence whose main verb is ἤλυθε at 251; the lines between describe the house. περικαλλέ’ is the accusative of περικαλλής ‘very fair’. ξεστῇς αἰθούσῃσι is a dative of means, ‘with polished colonnades’ (αἴθουσα, a roofed portico), and τετυγμένον is the perfect participle of τεύχω ‘make, build’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐν αὐτῷ
πεντήκοντ’ ἔνεσαν θάλαμοι ξεστοῖο λίθοιο
πλησίον ἀλλήλων δεδμημένοι, ἔνθα δὲ παῖδες
κοιμῶντο Πριάμοιο παρὰ μνηστῇς ἀλόχοισι,
sentences.tr:
autar en autōi
pentēkont’ enesan thalamoi xestoio lithoio
plēsion allēlōn dedmēmenoi, entha de paides
koimōnto Priamoio para mnēstēis alochoisi,
sentences.l:
but within it
fifty chambers were, of polished stone,
built close to one another, and there the sons
of Priam slept beside their wedded wives,
sentences.i: but inside it were fifty chambers of polished stone, built close to one another, and there Priam’s sons slept beside their wedded wives,
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of 243. αὐτὰρ ἐν αὐτῷ is ‘but in it’, and ἔνεσαν (= ἐνῆσαν) is ‘were in it’. ξεστοῖο λίθοιο is a genitive of material, ‘of polished stone’, and δεδμημένοι is the perfect passive participle of δέμω ‘build’. μνηστῇς ἀλόχοισι are ‘wooed’, that is lawfully married, wives; the Greek calls the men παῖδες Πριάμοιο ‘children of Priam’, and the wives show they are sons.

sentences.t:
κουράων δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐναντίοι ἔνδοθεν αὐλῆς
δώδεκ’ ἔσαν τέγεοι θάλαμοι ξεστοῖο λίθοιο
πλησίον ἀλλήλων δεδμημένοι, ἔνθα δὲ γαμβροὶ
κοιμῶντο Πριάμοιο παρ’ αἰδοίῃς ἀλόχοισιν·
sentences.tr:
kouraōn d’ heterōthen enantioi endothen aulēs
dōdek’ esan tegeoi thalamoi xestoio lithoio
plēsion allēlōn dedmēmenoi, entha de gambroi
koimōnto Priamoio par’ aidoiēis alochoisin·
sentences.l:
and on the other side, for the daughters, opposite, within the courtyard,
twelve roofed chambers were, of polished stone,
built close to one another, and there the sons-in-law
of Priam slept beside their revered wives;
sentences.i: and on the other side, facing them inside the courtyard, there were twelve roofed chambers of polished stone for his daughters, built close to one another, and there Priam’s sons-in-law slept beside their revered wives;
sentences.n: κουράων … ἑτέρωθεν ‘on the other side, for the daughters’ sets the second row against the sons’ chambers, and ἐναντίοι ‘opposite’ agrees with θάλαμοι. ἔσαν is ἦσαν ‘were’. τέγεοι ‘roofed’ comes from τέγος ‘roof’. γαμβροί are the husbands of Priam’s daughters, here ‘sons-in-law’. αἰδοίῃς, ‘revered’, is a dative plural in -ῃς, agreeing with ἀλόχοισιν.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά οἱ ἠπιόδωρος ἐναντίη ἤλυθε μήτηρ
Λαοδίκην ἐσάγουσα θυγατρῶν εἶδος ἀρίστην·
sentences.tr:
entha hoi ēpiodōros enantiē ēlythe mētēr
Laodikēn esagousa thygatrōn eidos aristēn·
sentences.l:
There to him gentle-giving came to meet him his mother,
Laodice leading in, in form the best of her daughters;
sentences.i: There his mother came to meet him, gentle in her giving, leading in Laodice, the best in form of her daughters;
sentences.n: His mother is Hecuba, not named until 293. ἠπιόδωρος is built from ἤπιος ‘gentle’ and δῶρον ‘gift’, and is rendered by its parts. ἐναντίη is ‘face to face, to meet him’, and ἤλυθε is the aorist ‘came’. ἐσάγουσα is the participle of ἐσάγω (= εἰσάγω) ‘lead in’; Λαοδίκην is her object. εἶδος ἀρίστην ‘best in form’ takes the genitive θυγατρῶν ‘of the daughters’.

sentences.t: ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρὶ ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.tr: en t’ ara hoi phy cheiri epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomaze·
sentences.l: And she clasped him by the hand, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: She took his hand, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: A formula for taking someone by the hand to speak: ἔν … φῦ is the aorist of ἐμφύω ‘grow into, cling to’, with the preverb separated from its verb, and χειρί is the hand held. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε ‘spoke a word and addressed him by name’ has ἔκ … ὀνόμαζε split the same way. The line stands also in the Odyssey, and its English is taken from there.

sentences.t: τέκνον τίπτε λιπὼν πόλεμον θρασὺν εἰλήλουθας;
sentences.tr: teknon tipte lipōn polemon thrasyn eilēlouthas;
sentences.l: “Child, why, having left bold war, have you come?
sentences.i: “Child, why have you come, leaving the bold war behind?
sentences.n: τέκνον ‘child’ is the vocative, said by a mother to a grown son. τίπτε is τί ποτε ‘why ever’. λιπών ‘having left’ is an aorist participle, and εἰλήλουθας is the perfect of ἔρχομαι, ‘you have come’. θρασύν ‘bold’ goes with πόλεμον and need not carry blame. The question mark is the Greek ;.

sentences.t:
ἦ μάλα δὴ τείρουσι δυσώνυμοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
μαρνάμενοι περὶ ἄστυ·
sentences.tr:
ē mala dē teirousi dysōnymoi huies Achaiōn
marnamenoi peri asty·
sentences.l:
Truly, very much so, wear down the ill-named sons of the Achaeans,
fighting around the town;
sentences.i: Surely the ill-named sons of the Achaeans are wearing us down hard, fighting round the town;
sentences.n: ἦ μάλα δή ‘truly, very much so’ opens her answer to her own question. τείρουσι is the present of τείρω ‘wear down, press hard’; no object is spoken, and ‘us’ (the Trojans) is supplied in the English. δυσώνυμοι ‘ill-named’ (δυσ- + ὄνομα) means their name is one of bad omen. μαρνάμενοι is the participle of μάρναμαι ‘fight’.

sentences.t:
σὲ δ’ ἐνθάδε θυμὸς ἀνῆκεν
ἐλθόντ’ ἐξ ἄκρης πόλιος Διὶ χεῖρας ἀνασχεῖν.
sentences.tr:
se d’ enthade thymos anēken
elthont’ ex akrēs polios Dii cheiras anaschein.
sentences.l:
and you here your spirit has sent,
having come, from the high city, hands to Zeus to lift up.
sentences.i: and your heart has urged you here to lift your hands to Zeus from the high city.
sentences.n: σὲ δ’ ἐνθάδε θυμὸς ἀνῆκεν is ‘and your spirit has sent you up here’, from ἀνίημι ‘send up, urge on’. ἐλθόντ’ is an accusative participle agreeing with σέ. ἐξ ἄκρης πόλιος ‘from the high city’ could hang on ἐλθόντ’ or on ἀνασχεῖν ‘to hold up’; the English takes it with the lifting of hands, since Hector has just come in from the plain.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μέν’ ὄφρά κέ τοι μελιηδέα οἶνον ἐνείκω,
ὡς σπείσῃς Διὶ πατρὶ καὶ ἄλλοις ἀθανάτοισι
πρῶτον, ἔπειτα δὲ καὐτὸς ὀνήσεαι αἴ κε πίῃσθα.
sentences.tr:
alla men’ ophra ke toi meliēdea oinon eneikō,
hōs speisēis Dii patri kai allois athanatoisi
prōton, epeita de kautos onēseai ai ke piēistha.
sentences.l:
But wait, until to you honey-sweet wine I bring,
so that you may pour to Zeus the father and to the other immortals
first, and then you yourself will profit, if you drink.
sentences.i: But wait until I bring you honey-sweet wine, so that you may first pour a libation to Father Zeus and the other immortals, and then you will profit from it yourself, if you drink.
sentences.n: μέν’ is the imperative μένε ‘wait’. ὄφρά κε … ἐνείκω ‘until I bring’ and ὡς σπείσῃς ‘so that you may pour a libation’ are aorist subjunctives; ὡς here means ‘so that’. μελιηδέα is ‘honey-sweet’. καὐτός is καὶ αὐτός ‘even you yourself’, ὀνήσεαι the future of ὀνίνημι ‘benefit’, and αἴ κε πίῃσθα ‘if you drink’ has the second-singular ending -σθα.

sentences.t:
ἀνδρὶ δὲ κεκμηῶτι μένος μέγα οἶνος ἀέξει,
ὡς τύνη κέκμηκας ἀμύνων σοῖσιν ἔτῃσι.
sentences.tr:
andri de kekmēōti menos mega oinos aexei,
hōs tynē kekmēkas amynōn soisin etēisi.
sentences.l:
For a man grown weary, great might wine increases,
as you have grown weary, defending your own kinsmen.”
sentences.i: For wine increases a weary man’s great might, as you have grown weary defending your own kinsmen.”
sentences.n: κεκμηῶτι is the dative perfect participle of κάμνω ‘be weary’, and μένος μέγα is ‘great might’. ἀέξει is ‘makes grow, increases’. τύνη is an emphatic epic form of σύ ‘you’, and κέκμηκας is the perfect ‘you have grown weary’. ἀμύνων ‘warding off’ takes the dative; ἔτῃσι is the dative plural of ἔτης ‘kinsman’, and σοῖσιν ‘your own’ agrees. Her speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ēmeibet’ epeita megas korythaiolos Hektōr·
sentences.l: Her then answered great Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: Then great Hector of the glancing helmet answered her:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ‘then he answered her’ is the usual line-opening for a reply, with ἠμείβετο the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι. Here the subject is μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ, ‘great Hector of the glancing helmet’ (κόρυς ‘helmet’ and αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’); the epithet is translated every time he has it.

sentences.t:
μή μοι οἶνον ἄειρε μελίφρονα πότνια μῆτερ,
μή μ’ ἀπογυιώσῃς μένεος, ἀλκῆς τε λάθωμαι·
sentences.tr:
mē moi oinon aeire meliphrona potnia mēter,
mē m’ apoguiōsēis meneos, alkēs te lathōmai·
sentences.l:
“Do not for me wine lift up, honey-hearted, lady mother,
lest you unnerve me of my might, and my might I forget;
sentences.i: “Do not bring me heart-sweetening wine, lady mother, or you may unnerve me and rob me of my might, and I may forget my might;
sentences.n: μή μοι … ἄειρε is a prohibition with the imperative of ἀείρω ‘lift, bring’. μελίφρονα (μέλι ‘honey’ + φρήν) is of uncertain sense, probably ‘sweet to the mind’; the house rendering is ‘honey-hearted’ in the Greek-order line and ‘heart-sweetening’ in the English. μή μ’ ἀπογυιώσῃς … λάθωμαι are two aorist subjunctives of fear, ‘lest you unnerve me … and I forget’; ἀπογυιόω takes the genitive μένεος and λανθάνομαι the genitive ἀλκῆς. Both μένος and ἀλκή are ‘might’ by house rule.

sentences.t:
χερσὶ δ’ ἀνίπτοισιν Διὶ λείβειν αἴθοπα οἶνον
ἅζομαι·
sentences.tr:
chersi d’ aniptoisin Dii leibein aithopa oinon
hazomai·
sentences.l:
With hands unwashed to Zeus to pour fire-faced wine
I am in awe;
sentences.i: I shrink from pouring the wine that has the look of fire to Zeus with unwashed hands;
sentences.n: χερσὶ δ’ ἀνίπτοισιν ‘with unwashed hands’ is a dative of means (ἄνιπτος, ‘not washed’). Διὶ λείβειν ‘to pour to Zeus’ is a libation. αἴθοπα οἶνον is ‘wine with the look of fire’ (αἴθω ‘burn’ + ὤψ ‘look’), and it is the object of λείβειν. ἅζομαι ‘I dread, I stand in awe of’ governs the infinitive, so the sense is that he fears to do it.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ πῃ ἔστι κελαινεφέϊ Κρονίωνι
αἵματι καὶ λύθρῳ πεπαλαγμένον εὐχετάασθαι.
sentences.tr:
oude pēi esti kelainepheï Kroniōni
haimati kai lythrōi pepalagmenon euchetaasthai.
sentences.l:
nor is it in any way possible to the dark-clouded son of Cronus,
with blood and gore spattered, to pray.
sentences.i: nor is it in any way possible for a man spattered with blood and gore to pray to the son of Cronus of the dark clouds.
sentences.n: οὐδέ πῃ ἔστι ‘nor is it in any way possible’ takes the infinitive εὐχετάασθαι, an epic form of εὔχεσθαι ‘pray’ with a stretched vowel. κελαινεφέϊ Κρονίωνι is the dative of the god prayed to; κελαινεφής is ‘dark-clouded’. αἵματι καὶ λύθρῳ are datives, ‘with blood and gore’, and πεπαλαγμένον is a perfect passive participle of παλάσσω ‘spatter’, agreeing with the unspoken man who prays.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν πρὸς νηὸν Ἀθηναίης ἀγελείης
ἔρχεο σὺν θυέεσσιν ἀολλίσσασα γεραιάς·
sentences.tr:
alla sy men pros nēon Athēnaiēs ageleiēs
ercheo syn thyeessin aollissasa geraias·
sentences.l:
But you to the temple of Athena the spoil-driver
go, with offerings, having gathered the old women;
sentences.i: But you go to the temple of Athena, the driver of spoil, with offerings, after gathering the old women;
sentences.n: σὺ μέν ‘but you, for your part’ is answered by ἐγὼ δέ at 280. νηόν is the Homeric form of ναός ‘temple’, and ἔρχεο is the imperative ‘go’. ἀγελείης ‘driver of spoil’ is Athena’s epithet; it is probably ἄγω + λεία, but its sense is not certain. θυέεσσιν ‘with offerings’ is from θύος, things burnt in sacrifice. ἀολλίσσασα is an aorist participle of ἀολλίζω ‘gather together’.

sentences.t:
πέπλον δ’, ὅς τίς τοι χαριέστατος ἠδὲ μέγιστος
ἔστιν ἐνὶ μεγάρῳ καί τοι πολὺ φίλτατος αὐτῇ,
τὸν θὲς Ἀθηναίης ἐπὶ γούνασιν ἠϋκόμοιο,
sentences.tr:
peplon d’, hos tis toi chariestatos ēde megistos
estin eni megarōi kai toi poly philtatos autēi,
ton thes Athēnaiēs epi gounasin ēÿkomoio,
sentences.l:
and a robe, whichever to you is most graceful and greatest
in the hall and by far dearest to you yourself,
that one lay on the knees of fine-haired Athena,
sentences.i: and the robe that is the most graceful and the greatest in your hall, and by far the dearest to you yourself, lay it on the knees of fine-haired Athena,
sentences.n: πέπλον … τὸν θές: the robe is named first and then picked up by τόν, ‘that one lay’. ὅς τίς τοι is ‘whichever to you’, with τοι = σοι. The three superlatives χαριέστατος, μέγιστος and φίλτατος say which robe; αὐτῇ ‘to you yourself’ means the one she herself values most. θές is the aorist imperative of τίθημι, ‘lay’. ἠϋκόμοιο ‘fine-haired’ is Athena’s stock epithet here.

sentences.t:
καί οἱ ὑποσχέσθαι δυοκαίδεκα βοῦς ἐνὶ νηῷ
ἤνις ἠκέστας ἱερευσέμεν, αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃ
ἄστύ τε καὶ Τρώων ἀλόχους καὶ νήπια τέκνα,
sentences.tr:
kai hoi hyposchesthai dyokaideka bous eni nēōi
ēnis ēkestas hiereusemen, ai k’ eleēsēi
asty te kai Trōōn alochous kai nēpia tekna,
sentences.l:
and to promise her twelve cows in the temple,
year-old, never-goaded, to sacrifice, if she will take pity on
the town and the Trojans’ wives and infant children,
sentences.i: and promise her twelve yearling heifers in the temple, never touched by the goad, to sacrifice, if she will take pity on the town and the wives of the Trojans and their little children,
sentences.n: These three lines repeat Helenus’ message to Hector at 6.93–95, word for word. ὑποσχέσθαι is an infinitive used as a command, ‘and promise’, and ἱερευσέμεν a future infinitive, ‘to sacrifice’. ἤνις is ‘a year old’. The sense of ἠκέστας is not known for certain; it is taken as ‘never goaded’. αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃ ‘if she will take pity’ has Athena as the one pitying.

sentences.t:
αἴ κεν Τυδέος υἱὸν ἀπόσχῃ Ἰλίου ἱρῆς
ἄγριον αἰχμητὴν κρατερὸν μήστωρα φόβοιο.
sentences.tr:
ai ken Tydeos huion aposchēi Iliou hirēs
agrion aichmētēn krateron mēstōra phoboio.
sentences.l:
if the son of Tydeus she will hold off from sacred Ilios,
the wild spearman, strong counsellor of flight.
sentences.i: if she will keep the son of Tydeus away from sacred Ilios, that wild spearman, strong master of flight.
sentences.n: αἴ κεν … ἀπόσχῃ ‘if she will hold off’ takes the genitive Ἰλίου ἱρῆς (ἱρός is ἱερός ‘sacred’). Τυδέος υἱόν is Diomedes, not named until 306. The next line is in apposition: ἄγριον ‘wild’, αἰχμητήν ‘spearman’, κρατερόν ‘strong’, μήστωρα φόβοιο. μήστωρ is ‘adviser, contriver’ and φόβος is ‘flight, rout’; the house English is ‘master of flight’, fixed at 6.96–97.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν πρὸς νηὸν Ἀθηναίης ἀγελείης
ἔρχευ, ἐγὼ δὲ Πάριν μετελεύσομαι ὄφρα καλέσσω
αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσ’ εἰπόντος ἀκουέμεν·
sentences.tr:
alla sy men pros nēon Athēnaiēs ageleiēs
ercheu, egō de Parin meteleusomai ophra kalessō
ai k’ ethelēis’ eipontos akouemen·
sentences.i: But you go to the temple of Athena, the driver of spoil, and I will go after Paris to summon him, if he will listen when I speak;
sentences.n: Line 279 repeats 269, and 280 has ἔρχευ, the contracted ἔρχεο of 270. ἐγὼ δέ answers σὺ μέν. μετελεύσομαι is the future of μετέρχομαι ‘go after’, and ὄφρα καλέσσω an aorist subjunctive of purpose. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσ’ ‘if he is willing’ has the infinitive ἀκουέμεν; εἰπόντος is the genitive of the speaker heard, ‘one who speaks’, here Hector himself.

sentences.t:
ὥς κέ οἱ αὖθι
γαῖα χάνοι·
sentences.tr:
hōs ke hoi authi
gaia chanoi·
sentences.l:
so for him right there
the earth might gape;
sentences.i: May the earth gape open for him right there;
sentences.n: ὥς κέ οἱ … γαῖα χάνοι is a wish: ὥς ‘so’, κε, and the optative χάνοι, from χάσκω ‘gape’. οἱ is ‘for him’ (Paris) and αὖθι ‘right there, on the spot’. The unit begins in the middle of 281.

sentences.t:
μέγα γάρ μιν Ὀλύμπιος ἔτρεφε πῆμα
Τρωσί τε καὶ Πριάμῳ μεγαλήτορι τοῖό τε παισίν.
sentences.tr:
mega gar min Olympios etrephe pēma
Trōsi te kai Priamōi megalētori toio te paisin.
sentences.l:
for a great woe the Olympian reared him
for the Trojans and for great-spirited Priam and his sons.
sentences.i: for the Olympian reared him as a great woe to the Trojans, to great-spirited Priam and to his sons.
sentences.n: Ὀλύμπιος, ‘the Olympian’, is Zeus left unnamed. ἔτρεφε is the imperfect of τρέφω ‘rear’, and πῆμα ‘woe’ stands in apposition to μιν ‘him’, as what he was reared to be. Τρωσί … Πριάμῳ … παισίν are datives of the ones harmed. μεγαλήτορι is ‘great-spirited’, and τοῖο is the old genitive of the article used as ‘his’. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
εἰ κεῖνόν γε ἴδοιμι κατελθόντ’ Ἄϊδος εἴσω
φαίην κε φρέν’ ἀτέρπου ὀϊζύος ἐκλελαθέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
ei keinon ge idoimi katelthont’ Aïdos eisō
phaiēn ke phren’ aterpou oïzyos eklelathesthai.
sentences.l:
If him at least I might see gone down into Hades’ house,
I would say that my mind had forgotten joyless distress.”
sentences.i: If I could see him gone down into the house of Hades, I would say that my mind had forgotten its joyless distress.”
sentences.n: εἰ … ἴδοιμι and φαίην κε are both optatives, ‘if I were to see … I would say’, a remote condition, close to a wish. κεῖνον is ‘that man’ (Paris), and κατελθόντ’ an aorist participle ‘gone down’. Ἄϊδος εἴσω ‘into Hades’ takes a genitive, with ‘house’ understood. ἐκλελαθέσθαι is a reduplicated aorist infinitive of ἐκλανθάνομαι, ‘to have forgotten’, with the genitive ἀτέρπου ὀϊζύος ‘joyless distress’. His speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, ἣ δὲ μολοῦσα ποτὶ μέγαρ’ ἀμφιπόλοισι
κέκλετο·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hē de molousa poti megar’ amphipoloisi
kekleto·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and she, having gone to the hall, to the attendants
called;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and she went to the hall and called to her attendants;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech, and ἣ δέ ‘and she’ is Hecuba. μολοῦσα is the aorist participle of βλώσκω ‘go, come’. ποτὶ μέγαρ’ ‘to the hall’ is a plural for the one room (ποτί = πρός). κέκλετο ‘called, summoned’ is an aorist of κέλομαι, and ἀμφιπόλοισι ‘attendants’ is its dative. The unit ends mid-line.

sentences.t: ταὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀόλλισσαν κατὰ ἄστυ γεραιάς.
sentences.tr: tai d’ ar’ aollissan kata asty geraias.
sentences.l: and they gathered through the town the old women.
sentences.i: and they gathered the old women through the town.
sentences.n: ταί is the article used as ‘they’, the attendants. ἀόλλισσαν is a past tense of ἀολλίζω ‘gather together’ with doubled σ, the verb of the order at 270 (ἀολλίσσασα). κατὰ ἄστυ ‘through the town’ shows them going from house to house. γεραιάς ‘old women’ are the elders of the city. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t: αὐτὴ δ’ ἐς θάλαμον κατεβήσετο κηώεντα,
sentences.tr: autē d’ es thalamon katebēseto kēōenta,
sentences.l: and herself into the chamber went down, fragrant,
sentences.i: and she herself went down into the fragrant chamber,
sentences.n: αὐτὴ δ’ ‘and she herself’ turns from the attendants to Hecuba. κατεβήσετο is an aorist middle of καταβαίνω, ‘went down’. ἐς θάλαμον is ‘into the chamber’, and κηώεντα is ‘fragrant’ (κηώεις). The next line says what is kept there: the robes.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἔσάν οἱ πέπλοι παμποίκιλα ἔργα γυναικῶν
Σιδονίων, τὰς αὐτὸς Ἀλέξανδρος θεοειδὴς
ἤγαγε Σιδονίηθεν ἐπιπλὼς εὐρέα πόντον,
τὴν ὁδὸν ἣν Ἑλένην περ ἀνήγαγεν εὐπατέρειαν·
sentences.tr:
enth’ esan hoi peploi pampoikila erga gynaikōn
Sidoniōn, tas autos Alexandros theoeidēs
ēgage Sidoniēthen epiplōs eurea ponton,
tēn hodon hēn Helenēn per anēgagen eupatereian·
sentences.l:
where were her robes, all-intricate works of Sidonian
women, whom Alexander himself, godlike in form,
brought from Sidon, having sailed over the wide sea,
on the journey on which he led away also Helen, daughter of a good father;
sentences.i: where her robes were, the all-intricate work of Sidonian women, whom Alexander himself, godlike in form, had brought from Sidon over the wide sea, on the voyage on which he also carried off Helen, daughter of a good father;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ἔσάν οἱ is ‘where there were to her’ (ἔσαν = ἦσαν). Alexander is Paris. τάς is feminine, so it refers to the Sidonian women (γυναικῶν Σιδονίων), the weavers, not to the robes. Σιδονίηθεν is ‘from Sidon’ (-θεν). ἐπιπλώς is a participle, ‘sailing over’, with εὐρέα πόντον ‘the wide sea’. περ is ‘also’; ἀνήγαγεν is ‘led away’ (ἀνάγω, ‘lead up’, is the verb for taking someone out to sea); εὐπατέρειαν is ‘daughter of a good father’.

sentences.t:
τῶν ἕν’ ἀειραμένη Ἑκάβη φέρε δῶρον Ἀθήνῃ,
ὃς κάλλιστος ἔην ποικίλμασιν ἠδὲ μέγιστος,
ἀστὴρ δ’ ὣς ἀπέλαμπεν·
sentences.tr:
tōn hen’ aeiramenē Hekabē phere dōron Athēnēi,
hos kallistos eēn poikilmasin ēde megistos,
astēr d’ hōs apelampen·
sentences.i: Hecuba lifted out one of them and carried it as a gift to Athena, the one that was the most beautiful in its intricate work and the largest, and it shone like a star;
sentences.n: τῶν ἕν’ is ‘one of them’ (the robes), ἀειραμένη ‘having lifted’, and Ἑκάβη φέρε ‘Hecuba carried’ (φέρε is an unaugmented imperfect). δῶρον is in apposition. ὅς is masculine, for the robe. κάλλιστος ἔην ποικίλμασιν ἠδὲ μέγιστος is a line the Odyssey uses of a robe of Helen’s, and its English is taken from there. ἀστὴρ δ’ ὣς ἀπέλαμπεν ‘it shone forth like a star’.

sentences.t: ἔκειτο δὲ νείατος ἄλλων.
sentences.tr: ekeito de neiatos allōn.
sentences.l: and it lay lowest of the others.
sentences.i: and it lay at the bottom of the rest.
sentences.n: ἔκειτο ‘it lay’ is the imperfect of κεῖμαι, and the robe is the subject. νείατος ‘lowest’ is a superlative, and ἄλλων is the genitive of the rest. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t: βῆ δ’ ἰέναι, πολλαὶ δὲ μετεσσεύοντο γεραιαί.
sentences.tr: bē d’ ienai, pollai de metesseuonto geraiai.
sentences.l: and she set out to go, and many old women hurried after.
sentences.i: She set out, and many old women hurried after her.
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἰέναι is ‘and she set out to go’: βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω, with the infinitive ἰέναι (εἶμι). μετεσσεύοντο is the imperfect middle of μετασεύομαι ‘hurry after’, with the σ doubled for the verse. πολλαὶ … γεραιαί ‘many old women’ are the ones gathered at 287.

sentences.t:
αἱ δ’ ὅτε νηὸν ἵκανον Ἀθήνης ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ,
τῇσι θύρας ὤϊξε Θεανὼ καλλιπάρῃος
Κισσηῒς ἄλοχος Ἀντήνορος ἱπποδάμοιο·
sentences.tr:
hai d’ hote nēon hikanon Athēnēs en polei akrēi,
tēisi thyras ōïxe Theanō kalliparēios
Kissēïs alochos Antēnoros hippodamoio·
sentences.i: And when they reached the temple of Athena in the high city, fair-cheeked Theano opened the doors for them, the daughter of Cisseus and wife of Antenor, tamer of horses;
sentences.n: αἱ δ’ ὅτε ‘and when they’ looks back to the women. ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ ‘in the high city’ is the citadel. τῇσι is the article used as ‘for them’, a dative. ὤϊξε is an aorist of ἀνοίγνυμι ‘open’. Κισσηΐς is a patronymic, ‘daughter of Cisseus’. Ἀντήνορος is genitive with ἄλοχος, and ἱπποδάμοιο ‘tamer of horses’ is his stock epithet. καλλιπάρῃος ‘fair-cheeked’ (παρειά ‘cheek’) is hers.

sentences.t: τὴν γὰρ Τρῶες ἔθηκαν Ἀθηναίης ἱέρειαν.
sentences.tr: tēn gar Trōes ethēkan Athēnaiēs hiereian.
sentences.l: for her the Trojans made priestess of Athena.
sentences.i: for the Trojans had made her priestess of Athena.
sentences.n: τὴν γάρ explains why Theano is the one who opens the doors: she is the priestess. ἔθηκαν is the aorist of τίθημι ‘put, make’, with two accusatives, τὴν … ἱέρειαν ‘her priestess’, and the genitive Ἀθηναίης names the goddess served. Τρῶες ‘Trojans’ is the subject.

sentences.t: αἳ δ’ ὀλολυγῇ πᾶσαι Ἀθήνῃ χεῖρας ἀνέσχον·
sentences.tr: hai d’ ololygēi pasai Athēnēi cheiras aneschon·
sentences.l: and they with a cry, all, to Athena lifted up their hands;
sentences.i: and all of them, with a cry, held up their hands to Athena;
sentences.n: αἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, with the article as pronoun, the women. ὀλολυγή is a loud cry raised by women when praying or at a sacrifice. ἀνέσχον is the aorist of ἀνέχω ‘hold up’, the verb Hecuba used of lifting hands to Zeus (ἀνασχεῖν, 257). Ἀθήνῃ is the Ionic dative, ‘to Athena’, and χεῖρας is the object.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἄρα πέπλον ἑλοῦσα Θεανὼ καλλιπάρῃος
θῆκεν Ἀθηναίης ἐπὶ γούνασιν ἠϋκόμοιο,
εὐχομένη δ’ ἠρᾶτο Διὸς κούρῃ μεγάλοιο·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ ara peplon helousa Theanō kalliparēios
thēken Athēnaiēs epi gounasin ēÿkomoio,
euchomenē d’ ērato Dios kourēi megaloio·
sentences.l:
And she, the robe having taken, Theano fair-cheeked,
laid it on the knees of fine-haired Athena,
and praying made her prayer to the daughter of great Zeus:
sentences.i: And fair-cheeked Theano took the robe and laid it on the knees of fine-haired Athena, and, praying, made her prayer to the daughter of great Zeus:
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ ἄρα ‘and she’, then named: Θεανώ. ἑλοῦσα is the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘take’. θῆκεν ‘laid’ with Ἀθηναίης ἐπὶ γούνασιν ἠϋκόμοιο is the line of 273 with the verb changed from the order to the deed. εὐχομένη … ἠρᾶτο has two verbs for praying, εὔχομαι and ἀράομαι, in one phrase. Διὸς κούρῃ μεγάλοιο ‘to the daughter of great Zeus’ is a dative and a formula.

sentences.t:
πότνι’ Ἀθηναίη ἐρυσίπτολι δῖα θεάων
ἆξον δὴ ἔγχος Διομήδεος, ἠδὲ καὶ αὐτὸν
πρηνέα δὸς πεσέειν Σκαιῶν προπάροιθε πυλάων,
sentences.tr:
potni’ Athēnaiē erysiptoli dia theaōn
axon dē enchos Diomēdeos, ēde kai auton
prēnea dos peseein Skaiōn proparoithe pylaōn,
sentences.l:
“Lady Athena, city-guarding, heavenly-one of goddesses,
break now the spear of Diomedes, and himself too
grant to fall headlong before the Scaean Gates,
sentences.i: “Lady Athena, guardian of the city, heavenly even among goddesses, break the spear of Diomedes, and grant that he himself also fall headlong before the Scaean Gates,
sentences.n: πότνι’ Ἀθηναίη ‘lady Athena’ is a vocative. ἐρυσίπτολι is formed from ἐρύομαι ‘protect’ and πτόλις (= πόλις) ‘city’, as is usually understood. δῖα θεάων ‘heavenly even among goddesses’ is the stock phrase. ἆξον is the aorist imperative of ἄγνυμι ‘break’; δός ‘grant’ takes the infinitive πεσέειν. πρηνέα ‘headlong’ agrees with αὐτόν. προπάροιθε takes the genitive Σκαιῶν … πυλάων.

sentences.t:
ὄφρά τοι αὐτίκα νῦν δυοκαίδεκα βοῦς ἐνὶ νηῷ
ἤνις ἠκέστας ἱερεύσομεν, αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃς
ἄστύ τε καὶ Τρώων ἀλόχους καὶ νήπια τέκνα.
sentences.tr:
ophra toi autika nyn dyokaideka bous eni nēōi
ēnis ēkestas hiereusomen, ai k’ eleēsēis
asty te kai Trōōn alochous kai nēpia tekna.
sentences.l:
so that to you at once now twelve cows in the temple,
year-old, never-goaded, we may sacrifice, if you will take pity on
the town and the Trojans’ wives and infant children.”
sentences.i: so that we may at once sacrifice to you in your temple twelve yearling heifers, never touched by the goad, if you will take pity on the town and the wives of the Trojans and their little children.”
sentences.n: ὄφρά τοι … ἱερεύσομεν is a purpose clause, ‘so that to you we may sacrifice’, and ἱερεύσομεν is an aorist subjunctive with a short vowel. It is the vow of 274–276 turned from third person (‘if she will take pity’) to second (αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃς ‘if you will take pity’), and so is the prayer’s offer. ἤνις ἠκέστας is ‘year-old, never-goaded’ again. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχομένη, ἀνένευε δὲ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’ euchomenē, aneneue de Pallas Athēnē.
sentences.l: So she spoke, praying, and signed a refusal Pallas Athena.
sentences.i: So she prayed, and Pallas Athena made a sign of refusal.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχομένη ‘so she spoke, praying’ closes the speech. ἀνένευε is the imperfect of ἀνανεύω, to throw the head back, the sign of ‘no’. The prayer is not granted, and the poet says so at once. Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη ‘Pallas Athena’ is the full name with its epithet; the meaning of Παλλάς is disputed.

sentences.t: ὣς αἳ μέν ῥ’ εὔχοντο Διὸς κούρῃ μεγάλοιο,
sentences.tr: hōs hai men rh’ euchonto Dios kourēi megaloio,
sentences.l: So they, then, were praying to the daughter of great Zeus,
sentences.i: So they were praying to the daughter of great Zeus,
sentences.n: ὣς αἳ μέν ‘so they, for their part’ is answered by Ἕκτωρ δέ in the next line. ῥ’ is ῥα, a particle; εὔχοντο is the imperfect of εὔχομαι ‘pray’, so the prayers go on while the scene turns. Διὸς κούρῃ μεγάλοιο is the same formula as in 304.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δὲ πρὸς δώματ’ Ἀλεξάνδροιο βεβήκει
καλά, τά ῥ’ αὐτὸς ἔτευξε σὺν ἀνδράσιν οἳ τότ’ ἄριστοι
ἦσαν ἐνὶ Τροίῃ ἐριβώλακι τέκτονες ἄνδρες,
sentences.tr:
Hektōr de pros dōmat’ Alexandroio bebēkei
kala, ta rh’ autos eteuxe syn andrasin hoi tot’ aristoi
ēsan eni Troiēi eribōlaki tektones andres,
sentences.i: while Hector went to the fine house of Alexander, which Alexander had built himself with the men who were then the best builders in Troy of the rich soil,
sentences.n: βεβήκει is a pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had gone’ in the sense of ‘was on his way’. δώματ’ is a plural for one house, and καλά ‘fine’ agrees with it. τά ῥ’ αὐτὸς ἔτευξε ‘which he himself made’, with Alexander as the maker. ἐριβώλακι ‘rich-soiled’ (ἐρι- ‘very’, βῶλος ‘clod’) goes with Τροίῃ. τέκτονες ἄνδρες ‘builder men’, that is craftsmen who work in wood, are in apposition to ἀνδράσιν.

sentences.t:
οἵ οἱ ἐποίησαν θάλαμον καὶ δῶμα καὶ αὐλὴν
ἐγγύθι τε Πριάμοιο καὶ Ἕκτορος ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ.
sentences.tr:
hoi hoi epoiēsan thalamon kai dōma kai aulēn
engythi te Priamoio kai Hektoros en polei akrēi.
sentences.l:
who made for him a chamber and a house and a courtyard
near Priam’s and Hector’s, in the high city.
sentences.i: who made him a chamber, a house and a courtyard near the houses of Priam and Hector, in the high city.
sentences.n: οἵ οἱ ἐποίησαν ‘who made for him’ has three objects, θάλαμον, δῶμα and αὐλήν: a bedchamber, a dwelling and a courtyard. ἐγγύθι τε Πριάμοιο καὶ Ἕκτορος has genitives after ἐγγύθι ‘near’, with ‘house’ left unsaid. ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ ‘in the high city’ is the same phrase as at 297.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ Ἕκτωρ εἰσῆλθε Διῒ φίλος, ἐν δ’ ἄρα χειρὶ
ἔγχος ἔχ’ ἑνδεκάπηχυ·
sentences.tr:
enth’ Hektōr eisēlthe Diï philos, en d’ ara cheiri
enchos ech’ hendekapēchy·
sentences.l:
There Hector went in, dear to Zeus, and in his hand
a spear he held, eleven-cubit;
sentences.i: There Hector, dear to Zeus, went in, with a spear eleven cubits long in his hand;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ … εἰσῆλθε ‘there he went in’. Διῒ φίλος ‘dear to Zeus’ is Hector’s stock epithet, translated every time. ἔχ’ is ἔχε, the imperfect ‘held’. ἑνδεκάπηχυ ‘eleven-cubit’ is built on πῆχυς, the forearm or cubit, a very long spear. The unit ends in the middle of 319, and the next picks up the same spear.

sentences.t:
πάροιθε δὲ λάμπετο δουρὸς
αἰχμὴ χαλκείη, περὶ δὲ χρύσεος θέε πόρκης.
sentences.tr:
paroithe de lampeto douros
aichmē chalkeiē, peri de chryseos thee porkēs.
sentences.l:
and in front gleamed of the spear
the point, bronze, and around it ran a golden ring.
sentences.i: and the bronze point of the spear gleamed in front, and a golden ring ran round it.
sentences.n: πάροιθε ‘in front’ and λάμπετο ‘gleamed’ describe the spear at the head. δουρός is the genitive of δόρυ ‘spear’, and αἰχμὴ χαλκείη ‘the bronze point’ is the subject. περὶ … θέε ‘ran round’ splits the verb περιθέω. χρύσεος πόρκης ‘a golden ring’ is the band round the head, which is what is generally understood. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ εὗρ’ ἐν θαλάμῳ περικαλλέα τεύχε’ ἕποντα
ἀσπίδα καὶ θώρηκα, καὶ ἀγκύλα τόξ’ ἁφόωντα·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ heur’ en thalamōi perikallea teuche’ heponta
aspida kai thōrēka, kai ankyla tox’ haphoōnta·
sentences.l:
Him he found in the chamber the very fair armour tending,
shield and breastplate, and the curved bow handling;
sentences.i: He found him in the chamber busy with his very fair armour, his shield and breastplate, and handling his curved bow;
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ εὗρ’ ‘and him he found’ has Hector as the unspoken subject. ἕποντα and ἁφόωντα are accusative participles, from ἕπω ‘be busy about, tend’ and ἁφάω ‘handle’. περικαλλέα ‘very fair’ goes with τεύχε’ ‘armour’, which the next line lists as shield and breastplate. ἀγκύλα τόξ’ ‘the curved bow’ has a plural for the one bow.

sentences.t:
Ἀργείη δ’ Ἑλένη μετ’ ἄρα δμῳῇσι γυναιξὶν
ἧστο καὶ ἀμφιπόλοισι περικλυτὰ ἔργα κέλευε.
sentences.tr:
Argeiē d’ Helenē met’ ara dmōiēisi gynaixin
hēsto kai amphipoloisi periklyta erga keleue.
sentences.l:
and Argive Helen among her maidservant women
sat, and for the attendants very famous works gave orders.
sentences.i: and Argive Helen sat among her maidservants and gave her attendants orders for their very famous work.
sentences.n: Ἀργείη δ’ Ἑλένη ‘and Argive Helen’ starts a second scene in the same room. μετ’ … δμῳῇσι γυναιξίν ‘among the maidservant women’ and ἧστο ‘sat’ (the old past of ἧμαι). κέλευε is the imperfect ‘she was ordering’, with the dative ἀμφιπόλοισι for the people told and the accusative ἔργα for what they are told to make. περικλυτά ‘very famous’ is περι- ‘very’ + κλυτός ‘famous’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ Ἕκτωρ νείκεσσεν ἰδὼν αἰσχροῖς ἐπέεσσι·
sentences.tr: ton d’ Hektōr neikessen idōn aischrois epeessi·
sentences.l: Him then Hector reviled, seeing him, with shameful words:
sentences.i: And Hector, seeing him, reviled him with shameful words:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ Ἕκτωρ νείκεσσεν ἰδὼν ‘Hector reviled him, seeing him’ is the line with which Hector began to rebuke Paris at 3.38. νείκεσσεν is the aorist of νεικέω ‘rebuke’, with σ doubled. αἰσχροῖς ἐπέεσσι is the dative plural of ἔπος, ‘with shameful words’, in its uncontracted epic form.

sentences.t: δαιμόνι’ οὐ μὲν καλὰ χόλον τόνδ’ ἔνθεο θυμῷ,
sentences.tr: daimoni’ ou men kala cholon tond’ entheo thymōi,
sentences.l: “Strange man, not at all fine is this anger you have put in your heart,
sentences.i: “Strange man, it is not fine, this anger you have put in your heart;
sentences.n: δαιμόνι’ is the vocative of δαιμόνιος ‘strange one’, a form of address whose force is uncertain, ‘strange one, driven by something beyond himself’. οὐ μὲν καλά is ‘not at all fine’, with καλά as a neuter predicate. χόλον τόνδ’ ‘this anger’; the line does not say what the anger is about. ἔνθεο is the aorist middle of ἐντίθημι, ‘you have put in’, and θυμῷ is the dative ‘in your heart’.

sentences.t:
λαοὶ μὲν φθινύθουσι περὶ πτόλιν αἰπύ τε τεῖχος
μαρνάμενοι·
sentences.tr:
laoi men phthinythousi peri ptolin aipy te teichos
marnamenoi·
sentences.l:
the people are perishing around the city and the steep wall,
fighting;
sentences.i: the people are dying round the city and its steep wall as they fight;
sentences.n: λαοὶ μὲν φθινύθουσι ‘the people are wasting away’; the μέν looks ahead to σέο δ’ in the next unit. πτόλιν is the epic form of πόλιν ‘city’. αἰπύ τεῖχος ‘steep wall’ is αἰπύ the neuter of αἰπύς. μαρνάμενοι is the participle ‘fighting’. The unit ends in the middle of 328.

sentences.t:
σέο δ’ εἵνεκ’ ἀϋτή τε πτόλεμός τε
ἄστυ τόδ’ ἀμφιδέδηε·
sentences.tr:
seo d’ heinek’ aÿtē te ptolemos te
asty tod’ amphidedēe·
sentences.l:
and because of you the battle-cry and the war
this town has blazed around;
sentences.i: and it is on your account that the battle-cry and the war have blazed up around this town;
sentences.n: σέο is the epic genitive of σύ, and εἵνεκ’ (= ἕνεκα) means ‘because of’. ἀϋτή is the ‘battle-cry’ and πτόλεμος the epic form of πόλεμος ‘war’. ἀμφιδέδηε is a perfect of ἀμφιδαίω ‘blaze around’ with the object ἄστυ τόδ’; the two subjects take one singular verb. The unit begins and ends mid-line.

sentences.t:
σὺ δ’ ἂν μαχέσαιο καὶ ἄλλῳ,
ὅν τινά που μεθιέντα ἴδοις στυγεροῦ πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
sy d’ an machesaio kai allōi,
hon tina pou methienta idois stygerou polemoio.
sentences.l:
and you would fight with another too,
whomever you might see slackening from hateful war.
sentences.i: and you would fight with another man too, whomever you might see slackening from hateful war.
sentences.n: σὺ δ’ ἂν μαχέσαιο καὶ ἄλλῳ is an optative with ἄν, ‘you would fight with another too’; μάχομαι takes the dative. ὅν τινά που … ἴδοις ‘whomever perhaps you might see’ is a second optative. μεθιέντα is the participle of μεθίημι ‘slacken from’, which takes the genitive στυγεροῦ πολέμοιο ‘hateful war’. The point is that Paris himself would quarrel with any other man he saw holding back. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄνα μὴ τάχα ἄστυ πυρὸς δηΐοιο θέρηται.
sentences.tr: all’ ana mē tacha asty pyros dēïoio therētai.
sentences.l: But up, lest soon the town with hostile fire be set ablaze.”
sentences.i: But up, or soon the town will be set ablaze with hostile fire.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄνα ‘but up!’ uses ἄνα as a shortened imperative (for ἀνάστηθι). μὴ τάχα … θέρηται is a clause of fear, ‘lest soon the town be burned’, with θέρηται the subjunctive of θέρομαι ‘be heated, burn’. πυρὸς δηΐοιο ‘by hostile fire’ is a genitive with θέρηται. His speech ends here.
